_readme: Compare languages page. Read from the CPDD guides and syllabuses on the department's drive, 6 Nov 2026, by four readers, with the main claims rechecked by script. Paraphrased: MOE text is not reproduced. Page numbers are PDF pages. c=m marks a finding based on term searches and sampled units. MTL B is left out under the hub rule.

about.what: What is distinctive about the Chinese, Malay and Tamil curriculum packages, how ML's STAR activity works, and what all three share.
points: What each language's CPDD package has that the other two do not.
STAR explained stage by stage, with a worked lesson.
Ten things all three languages share, and how each one carries them out.
about.use: Tap a feature to see where it is in the guides and how the other two languages compare.

lead: All three languages sit under one MTL syllabus framework, but CPDD built each package differently. This page sets out what is particular to each, then what they have in common. To see which practices a language could borrow, go to Learn across languages.

distinct.title: What is distinctive about each language
distinct.sub: Distinctive means we searched the other two languages' syllabuses and guides, in their own languages and in English, and did not find the same thing. Many of these differ in how a shared idea is built, not in whether it exists at all, so each one says what the others do instead.

CL.name: Chinese Language
CL.gist: A fixed unit template, the same in every unit, built around character learning.

items.n: Separate targets for reading and writing characters
items.line: The syllabus sets, for each course, how many characters students should recognise, a smaller number to write by hand, and a word total.
items.where: CL syllabus pp. 20 and 22. G1, for example, is about 1,500 to 1,600 characters read, 1,000 to 1,100 written and 3,000 words.
items.others: ML and TL list vocabulary lesson by lesson, but we found no numeric targets in their syllabuses.

items.n: Goals set out course by course, skill by skill
items.line: A table for each language skill shows how the target changes from G1 to Higher.
items.where: CL syllabus pp. 17 to 23.
items.others: ML's syllabus has one list of outcomes for the end of secondary school. TL's has no skill grid by course.

items.n: Listening and speaking lead the unit in G1
items.t: 听说在前, 读写在后
items.line: The syllabus suggests this order for G1 materials, so that oral work drives reading and writing. G2, G3 and Higher open with reading.
items.where: CL syllabus pp. 11 and 35. The unit tables of the G1 to Higher guides follow it.
items.others: ML's sample schemes of work often open a part with listening, but we found no rule that separates the courses. TL states no such order.

items.n: Pinyin typing as a taught block in G1
items.line: G1 has a block before writing that teaches typing and pinyin spelling, including telling similar sounds apart.
items.where: G1 guides, for example G1 1A pp. 16 to 17. It is in no G2, G3 or Higher guide.
items.others: TL teaches typing as an early, occasional activity. In ML, the typing mentions we read are SLS submission instructions.

items.n: Three readings of every core text
items.line: A named routine: the first read clears words and gets the gist, the second digs into structure and meaning, and the third consolidates and leads to writing.
items.where: All 24 G1 to Higher guides. Explained in G3 1A pp. 10 to 12.
items.others: We found no named re-reading routine in ML or TL. TL's named method is the Directed Reading Thinking Activity, which is about predicting and checking.

items.n: A separate culture lesson in every unit
items.line: Each unit has its own timed culture lesson, with four declared types of cultural content.
items.where: Every unit in the unit tables. Explained in G3 1A pp. 20 to 21.
items.others: Culture itself is shared. ML places culture notes inside each part (Santun Budaya) and tags them to Arif Budiman. TL has whole culture units and a short interest block in some units.

items.n: An integrated task closing every unit
items.line: Each unit ends with a real-world task that combines its skills. It is set in class, done mostly outside it, then shared.
items.where: Every unit in the unit tables. Explained in G3 1A pp. 22 to 23.
items.others: ML and TL have group tasks, but no fixed closing slot for one. TL's fixed closer is a reflection and teacher feedback.

items.n: Extensive reading built into each unit
items.t: 广泛阅读, 阅读护照
items.line: Time is set aside in each unit for free reading from a levelled series, with viewing options and a reading log called a passport.
items.where: All 24 guides. Explained in G3 1A pp. 24 to 26.
items.others: ML's syllabus has a school-run wide reading programme, which we did not find in its guides. TL's nearest is a set literature block with e-book stories.

items.n: A real-life text opens the reading block
items.line: Reading starts with a short text such as a timetable or route map, which seeds the theme and the reading skill and carries words that normal prose cannot.
items.where: Every unit in the unit tables. Explained in G3 1A p. 19.
items.others: All three use real-life texts. The difference is this fixed opening slot.

items.n: Short skill animations for each unit
items.line: Each unit's reading and writing skills have an explainer animation using examples from the core text, with advice on when to play it.
items.where: All 24 guides, for example G3 1A p. 15.
items.others: In ML and TL guides, the videos we read are about topics or stories, not a skills series. We did not open the SLS media themselves.

also: A method for setting 21CC unit goals
One named reading skill per unit
Say it, write it, check it (G1)

ML.name: Malay Language
ML.gist: A package framed by a model of the person, by language functions and by named teaching activities.

items.n: The STAR teaching activity
items.t: Analisis Senario, Inkuiri Berpasukan, Aplikasi, Refleksi
items.line: A four-stage activity in which teams work through a real situation. It is in no CL or TL guide or syllabus.
items.where: ML syllabus, Appendix E, and four G2 and G3 lessons.
items.others: Not named in any CL or TL guide or syllabus. It has not spread within ML either: we did not find it in G1 or Higher.

items.n: A named model of the learner
items.line: The syllabus vision describes a person with eight traits, tied to five culture and value categories. Units and schemes of work are mapped to them.
items.where: ML syllabus, including Appendix C. The values column in the sample schemes of work.
items.others: The name is in no CL or TL file. CL has culture categories and TL tags values on activities, but neither sets out a model of the person. Spread is uneven within ML.

items.n: Units built on six language functions
items.line: The books are based on six functions, such as expressing, regulating others and imagining. Each lesson and scheme of work row names one or more.
items.where: ML syllabus, Appendix D. 36 of the 39 ML files.
items.others: CL organises by skill point. We found no function framework in TL, though our Tamil search terms were our own translations.

items.n: Proverbs as a taught strand, with the meaning withheld
items.line: The syllabus gives proverbs their own section. Meanings are in the teacher guide but not the textbook, students work them out by discussion, and teachers are told to avoid memorising.
items.where: ML syllabus section 2.5. Explained at the start of the G3 1A guide.
items.others: All three teach set phrases. CL lists them as one type of language culture, and TL gives lists in its syllabus, with the teacher explaining the meanings in the lesson we read.

items.n: Lesson steps headed by Singapore Teaching Practice areas
items.line: Lesson steps carry teaching-area names such as activating prior knowledge, and appendices explain teaching activities step by step.
items.where: All 24 ML guides.
items.others: All three syllabuses use the Singapore Teaching Practice. CL guides use their own lesson flow (引学练用评). The TL lesson files we read use introduction, development and assessment steps.

items.n: The classroom as a formal language setting
items.line: Guides ask teachers to model High Malay and to train students to use it in class discussion.
items.where: 23 ML guides, for example G3 1A.
items.others: TL goes the other way: its syllabus wants spoken Tamil as the main classroom language. CL has one line on teachers keeping their language standard.

items.n: Sample schemes of work with assessment on each row
items.line: A sample plan by unit part, with the week, function, value, outcome, experiences, materials, and the assessment tool and success criteria.
items.where: 8 sample files, Sec 1 only, four courses.
items.others: TL's overviews are the closest match, with no assessment column. We found no file named as a scheme of work in CL or TL. CL gives rubrics and checklists in its guides.

items.n: Sample assessment weightings in the syllabus
items.line: The syllabus shows sample splits of weighted assessments and exams across the terms, with and without a mid-year exam.
items.where: ML syllabus p. 35.
items.others: We found no WA weighting figures in the CL or TL syllabus.

items.n: One document comparing all courses, with a Big Idea per unit
items.line: A single table sets each course's title, big idea, theme and intended understanding side by side.
items.where: The ML overview files for Sec 1B and Sec 4.
items.others: We found no side-by-side document in CL or TL. Their overviews and guides are per course.

also: Inquiry tasks flagged for weighted assessment

TL.name: Tamil Language
TL.gist: A package built on two forms of the language, published language lists and a detailed activity map.

items.n: Spoken Tamil as a taught form and the classroom language
items.line: The syllabus describes Tamil as having two forms, spoken and written, and wants spoken Tamil to be the main language of the classroom. Teachers show the differences between them.
items.where: TL syllabus pp. 11, 17 and 22 to 23. Stronger in G1 and G2 overviews than in G3 and Higher.
items.others: ML takes close to the opposite stance, with High Malay in class. In the CL hits we read, spoken practice is not treated as a separate form of the language.

items.n: Named idioms and paired words listed in the syllabus
items.line: Two appendices list the items by name, course and year, for example 80 idioms for G3 and 112 for Higher. Overview rows then cite them.
items.where: TL syllabus pp. 61 to 68.
items.others: CL and ML teach set phrases too, but we found no list in their syllabuses. ML warns against memorising lists.

items.n: A 72-item grammar chart, year by year
items.line: One chart marks each topic as new or as revision for Sec 1 to 4, including the rules for how sounds join between words.
items.where: TL syllabus, Appendix 3, pp. 57 to 60.
items.others: All three teach grammar inside units. ML's syllabus lists categories with no year map, and CL's makes general statements.

items.n: One classical work returning across courses and years
items.line: The Thirukkural recurs as a named activity, with verses cited by number. The teacher explains the meaning and students discuss it.
items.where: G1, G2, G3 and Higher overviews and lessons, mostly Sec 1 to 3. For example verses 631 and 634 in G3 Sec 3 Unit 3.
items.others: CL and ML have classical content too, such as 古诗 and pantun. The difference is one work returning repeatedly, with verse references. We searched named works, not every title.

items.n: Units about the Tamil language itself
items.line: The same sub-themes appear across courses at Sec 1 Unit 3 and Sec 3 Unit 7, so students study the language they are learning.
items.where: G1, G2, G3 and Higher overviews.
items.others: As a unit, ML has this in Higher only, as far as our searches show. No CL unit title is about the language, but our CL text search was not conclusive.

items.n: A timetabled reflection and teacher feedback closing each unit
items.line: Students fill in a reflection, then the teacher gives feedback, as rows with their own time in the overview.
items.where: TL overviews and most lesson files.
items.others: CL and ML have reflection at task level. ML lessons have a closing step, but we found no unit-end feedback row.

items.n: A fixed three-step card for every activity
items.t: பாட அறிமுகம், பாட வளர்ச்சி, மதிப்பீட்டு நடவடிக்கை
items.line: Each activity runs through an introduction, development, and an assessment task done in class.
items.where: TL lesson files, all courses. The assessment step is in 96 of the 141 TL files, which include Word and PDF copies.
items.others: CL has a fixed closing step for each block, mostly homework and preview. ML has headed lesson steps, with assessment as teacher judgment.

items.n: Research-named reading and discussion procedures
items.line: Lesson files name procedures such as the Directed Reading Thinking Activity, PQ4R, Reciprocal Teaching and Snowball Discussion, though no set recurs across courses.
items.where: About 30 of the 97 lesson files.
items.others: CL uses none of these English names. ML names Reciprocal Teaching in G1 and G2 Sec 3. An unnamed equivalent could still exist.

star.title: How STAR works
star.sub: STAR is a teaching activity that appears only in the Malay package. Students start from a real situation, investigate it in teams, use what they found, then reflect.
star.isnot: The ML guides call STAR a teaching activity, not a full inquiry framework. The ML syllabus lists it under activating prior knowledge in its Singapore Teaching Practice appendix, although the guides also use it in the middle of a lesson. This site groups it with inquiry because of what students do in it. That grouping is the department's reading, not CPDD's.
star.example: Worked example: G3 Sec 3 Unit 1, on stereotypes, prejudice and discrimination (ML guide, PDF pp. 24 to 26)

stages.does: The teacher gives a real situation. Students think it through and say what they already know or believe.
stages.ex: Groups look at images raising issues of gender, race, class, mother tongue and age. They answer yes or no to a question on each, backing it with stories they have read or lived.

stages.does: Teams look for information and raise their own questions. The teacher guides and confirms understanding.
stages.ex: Students read an infographic, discuss in groups how the three terms differ and what still confuses them, and search online for more. Each group reports back, then the teacher confirms the meanings.

stages.does: Teams use what they found on the situation or on a new one.
stages.ex: Groups go back to the images, decide which term each one shows, and explain why.

stages.does: Students think about what it means more widely and for themselves.
stages.ex: Groups consider why these things happen and how to stop them. Each student then records a personal view in SLS.

star.steps: The G3 1B guide also gives the teacher's steps: explain the activity and its purpose, give the scenario, allow time to think and analyse, invite students to share and explain, then build or clarify their understanding as the lesson goes on (appendix, PDF pp. 67 to 68).
uses: A simplified action plan based on STAR, used in groups to solve a village's problem and give instructions in order (PDF pp. 44 to 46).
Dilemma cards for groups of 4 or 5, worked through with a decision guide, with responses posted online (PDF pp. 44 to 45).
Groups of four design a class T-shirt, present their reasons and take feedback using sentence stems (PDF pp. 15 to 16).
The fullest model, with all four stages written out (PDF pp. 24 to 26).
star.note: CPDD names STAR in the lesson plans of these four units. This site also tags G3 1B Unit 8, because the appendix that prints STAR's steps covers Units 5 to 8, but no Unit 8 lesson plan names it.

shared.title: What all three languages share
shared.sub: A similarity is listed only if we found it in all three languages' own syllabus or guides, not just in the shared MTL framework. Each language carries it out in its own way, and we say where it is uneven.

items.n: The same three goals: communication, culture, connection
items.line: All three syllabuses name the same three purposes for learning the mother tongue, each in its own language.
items.ML: Komunikasi, Budaya, Hubungan, under the Arif Budiman vision (syllabus pp. 4 and 8).
items.TL: கருத்துப்பரிமாற்றம், பண்பாடு, தொடர்பிணைப்பு, under the aim of keeping Tamil a living language (syllabus pp. 5 to 8).

items.n: Communication through six language skills
items.line: All three teach listening, speaking, reading and writing, plus spoken and written interaction.
items.CL: 口语互动 and 书面互动, with outcomes for each course (syllabus p. 14).
items.ML: Interaksi Lisan and Interaksi Penulisan, built on six language functions (syllabus pp. 20 to 21).
items.watch: TL guides rarely use the written interaction label, even where the task is an email.

items.n: Values taught through content, not as a separate lesson
items.line: All three treat building character as part of language learning, and carry values through texts and tasks.
items.CL: 情意品德, developed through texts (syllabus pp. 8 and 29). For example, Unit 1 of G3 1A sets understanding responsibility as a reading objective.
items.ML: Arif Budiman values, tagged by unit in the guides and in a column of the sample schemes of work (syllabus pp. 14 to 15).
items.TL: விழுமியங்கள், built into activities through stories and experience (syllabus pp. 13 to 14), and tagged on activities in G1, G2 and Higher.
items.watch: The commitment is shared, but the list of values is not: we did not find the same set of six in all three. The word for values appears in none of the 38 TL G3 files.

items.n: Culture built into the language course
items.line: All three teach their own heritage and also build awareness of other cultures.
items.CL: 文化站 in each unit, with four types of cultural content.
items.ML: Five culture and value strands (syllabus pp. 14 to 15), with Santun Budaya notes in the guides.
items.TL: பண்பாட்டுக் கூறுகள் taught through discussion (syllabus p. 15), and units such as Pongal in Sec 1 Unit 2.
items.watch: We did not find a named category scheme for culture in the parts of the TL syllabus we read.

items.n: Literature and traditional sayings
items.line: All three use literary texts for enjoyment and teach traditional language such as idioms and proverbs.
items.CL: 广泛阅读 and 熟语 within language culture.
items.ML: A Sastera component in each unit, and Peribahasa.

items.n: News and real-world materials
items.line: All three bring current affairs and authentic texts into lessons, using local media.
items.CL: 新闻语料 from 8视界 and 早报校园, sorted by student level.
items.ML: Ehwal Semasa, using Berita Harian and BERITAMediacorp.

items.n: Technology and the Student Learning Space
items.line: All three build ICT into materials and lessons, and their guides point teachers to SLS resources.
items.CL: SLS lesson packs, skill animations and online peer review.
items.ML: e-Pedagogi and blended learning, with guides asking at each planning step whether students need SLS.
items.TL: ICT tags on activities, and e-books on SLS.
items.watch: The figures differ. The framework says about 30% of the curriculum, CL says 20 to 30% of materials, ML says 20 to 30% of time, and we found no figure in the TL syllabus.

items.n: Assessment that supports learning
items.line: All three call for a balance of formative and summative assessment, and use checklists or rubrics with students.
items.CL: 自评 and 互评 (syllabus pp. 31 to 32), and writing checklists.
items.ML: Penilaian Seimbang (syllabus pp. 35 to 36), with self-assessment checklists, peer assessment and rubrics.
items.TL: கற்றலுக்கான மதிப்பீடு (syllabus p. 52), with student reflection and teacher feedback.
items.watch: Peer assessment is thin in TL G3: the exact phrase is in 3 of 38 files.

items.n: The Singapore Teaching Practice as the teaching frame
items.line: All three take the Singapore Teaching Practice as their reference, and promote learner-centred and collaborative learning.
items.CL: 新加坡课堂教学实践要领, carried out through 引学练用评 (syllabus p. 28).
items.ML: The 24 teaching areas (syllabus pp. 27 to 29), with collaborative pedagogy and Think-Pair-Share.
items.TL: The 24 teaching areas (syllabus pp. 36 to 41), with கூடிக்கற்றல்.
items.watch: TL lesson plans rarely use the Singapore Teaching Practice labels, even though its syllabus sets them out.

items.n: Courses at different levels, with themes that widen from the self
items.line: Students take courses at different levels, and materials are organised by theme, moving outward from the self.
items.CL: Six theme areas (syllabus p. 35). Sec 1 and 2 core unit titles are mostly the same across courses.
items.ML: Three domains, from the personal to the region and world (syllabus p. 15). Unit titles differ by course.
items.TL: Six areas from self to world (syllabus p. 17). Many Sec 1 themes repeat across courses.
items.watch: The ML syllabus does not name the courses, so its course structure comes from the guide folders.

shared.notcounted: Not counted as shared: 21CC. All three syllabuses align with it, but the guides differ sharply. TL tags it activity by activity, CL explains a method with one worked unit, and ML has teacher notes in only one G1 Sec 4 guide. See Learn across languages.

method: What was read: the four syllabuses (the MTL, CL and ML syllabuses and most of TL), plus front matter and sample units of the guides across courses. The rest was term searches across every CL, ML and TL guide file on the department's drive, on 6 Nov 2026. The main claims were then rechecked by script.
Not found means not named in the documents. Teachers may well do these things in class, and a term search can miss an unnamed practice.
“Partly checked” marks a finding that rests on term searches and sampled units, not a full reading.

Limits: textbooks and workbooks are not on the drive, so these findings come from the guides and syllabuses. SLS was not opened for this page. A few Tamil words in the searchable copies are wrong, so a Tamil zero is strong but not absolute. Page numbers are PDF pages, and nothing here has been checked by the language teams yet.
File counts include copies. TL's 141 files include Word and PDF versions of the same guide.
